title: Bad luck, on schedule: the Carlos Vega file
excerpt: Five wrecks. Familiar passengers. Familiar paperwork. When does bad luck start looking like a business model?
note: Read the collisions together, not one at a time.

sections.label: 01 / THE HOOK
sections.heading: Carlos Vega has terrible luck.
sections.body:
Five wrecks in five years. Two rear-end collisions. One nighttime rollover. One hit while parked. One intersection crash involving a witness who somehow knew Carlos before the police arrived.

Every time, Carlos walked away. Every time, a claim followed. And every time, the details were just plausible enough to look ordinary when viewed alone.

The problem starts when you put the files next to each other: the same repair shop, the same medical clinic, repeated passengers, similar injury language, vehicles acquired shortly before crashes, claims filed quickly, and photographs taken even faster.

Carlos says he is simply unlucky. The pattern says otherwise.

sections.label: 02 / EDITORIAL
sections.heading: Accident is a comforting word.
sections.body:
It means nobody planned it. Nobody wanted it. Nobody looked at a guardrail, a parking lot, or another car and saw a payday.

Carlos’s fictional file becomes interesting not because any single collision is impossible, but because the same kinds of coincidences keep showing up around him.

Insurance fraud rarely arrives wearing a sign that says fraud. It usually looks like paperwork: a sore neck, a damaged bumper, a witness, a tow bill, a story ordinary enough to be believed.

Sometimes the most revealing evidence is not a smoking gun. It is repetition.

sections.label: 03 / COLLISION TIMELINE
sections.heading: Five accidents. One increasingly familiar cast.

items.title: Crash #1 — rear-ended
items.text: Carlos reports shoulder pain. The car is repaired. Nothing about the claim appears extraordinary on its own.

items.title: Crash #2 — nighttime intersection
items.text: Elena Ruiz is riding with Carlos. Both make injury claims. The same clinic appears in the paperwork.

items.title: Crash #3 — rollover
items.text: Carlos is driving a car owned by Mateo Silva. He says he swerved to avoid an animal. No independent witness is identified.

items.title: Crash #4 — hit while parked
items.text: Carlos reports a hit-and-run. Elena later appears in the related injury paperwork.

items.title: Crash #5 — low-speed collision
items.text: A witness backs Carlos’s account. A later records check links that witness to Mateo.

items.title: Pattern review begins
items.text: An insurer stops reading the claims one at a time and starts comparing names, clinics, vehicles, and dates.

items.title: The stories stop matching
items.text: Separate accounts that sounded plausible alone begin to conflict when investigators place them side by side.

sections.label: 04 / CASE ANALYSIS
sections.heading: The pattern is the story.
sections.body:
Pattern 01 — Frequency
Five claimed collisions in roughly five years would not prove fraud. It would, however, give an investigator a reason to compare the files rather than treating each event as isolated.

Pattern 02 — Familiar faces
Three crashes include one of the same two passengers. Real staged-collision schemes can involve coordinated drivers, passengers, and witnesses assigned different roles from claim to claim.

Pattern 03 — Medical claims
The fictional treatment records repeatedly route through the same clinic for similar soft-tissue complaints. Repetition is not proof of wrongdoing, but it is exactly the kind of relationship investigators would map.

Pattern 04 — The cars
Carlos favors inexpensive used vehicles purchased or insured shortly before incidents. Ownership dates, coverage changes, prior damage, repair invoices, and salvage history could become important context.

Pattern 05 — The helpful witness
The fifth collision becomes the hinge point: a supposedly independent witness later turns out to have a connection to someone already in the file.

people.name: Carlos Vega
people.bio: 38. Freelance auto-detailer. Charming, cooperative, and unusually fluent in the mechanics of a claim. He tends to have photographs and paperwork ready before anyone asks.

people.name: Elena Ruiz
people.bio: Carlos’s cousin. Appears in Crash #2, #4, and #5, with similar injury complaints appearing more than once.

people.name: Mateo Silva
people.bio: Owns the vehicle in Crash #3 and appears in the orbit of the witness from Crash #5. His role changes from file to file.

people.name: Dr. Adrian Bell
people.bio: Appears repeatedly in treatment records. The file makes no allegation of misconduct; repeated appearance alone is not evidence of wrongdoing.

people.name: Nina Park
people.bio: The person who stops reading five accidents and starts reading one story.
